text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Statement on Automated Takedown of Its Instagram Posts by Meta

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

text:
Question to X and Indian Authorities
Why did multiple X posts display the message “Due to local regulations, this content is restricted on X” when viewed from India?

Screenshots taken on 12 September 2026 show this message on multiple posts related to the BRICS Summit 2026, including posts by journalist Sidhant Sibal, Sarbananda Sonowal, and ANI concerning the summit, Cyril Ramaphosa’s arrival, and Xi Jinping’s arrival in Delhi.

For clarity, the screenshots document that the restriction message was displayed during a specific period on 12 September 2026. This post does not claim that the content remained restricted permanently, nor does it establish who initiated the restriction.

The screenshots by themselves do not establish whether the restriction resulted from an Indian government request, a court order, another legal process, X’s own compliance mechanism, or any other regulatory basis.

Therefore, I would like to ask @X @HMOIndia @PMOIndia @MIB_India @GoI_MeitY for clarification:

1• What specific law, rule, regulation, legal order, or other legal process formed the basis for restricting access to these posts in India during that period?

2• Was the restriction imposed following a request, direction, order, or other legal process from an Indian authority, or was it based on another mechanism?

3• If an Indian authority was involved, which authority issued or requested the restriction, subject to any applicable confidentiality requirements?

4• Was there a specific restriction order, written direction, court order, or other legal document relating to these posts?

5• If Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 was the applicable legal basis, can the relevant provision and applicable procedure be identified?

6• If Section 69A was not the basis, what specific legal or regulatory mechanism applied?

7• What does X mean by “local regulations” in these particular notices? Does the phrase specifically refer to Indian law or to another applicable regulatory requirement?

Why this question matters

This post is not alleging wrongdoing, censorship, or improper conduct by any individual, government authority, X, or any other organisation.

The purpose is simply to seek clarity and transparency about the legal or regulatory basis for a temporary restriction that was visible to users in India.

Where legally permissible, users should be able to understand what legal basis applied, whether an authority requested or directed the restriction, what process was followed, and why the restriction applied to the specific posts during that particular period.

text:
🧌free speech 🎤 

In Indian Polity, Freedom of Speech and Expression comes under:

➡️ Fundamental Rights → Article 19(1)(a)
➡️ Part III of the Constitution

Article 19(1)(a): All citizens have the right to freedom of speech and expression.

But this right is not absolute. Under Article 19(2), the State can impose reasonable restrictions on specified grounds:

➡️ Sovereignty and integrity of India
➡️ Security of the State
➡️ Friendly relations with foreign States
➡️ Public order
➡️ Decency or morality
➡️ Contempt of court
➡️ Defamation
➡️ Incitement to an offence

📌 Important distinction

Freedom of speech ≠ freedom to say anything without legal consequences.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

‘Meta Seems to Be Using the Excuse of Glitches’ - Supreme Court of India Senior Advocate, @sanjayuvacha

Safe harbour provision allows platforms to maintain status and not be responsible for user generated content ‘as long as it abides by lawful directives given by the govt, Sanjay Hegde tells RT India.

Can courts force Google and Meta to stop illegal uploads before they're even reported? That's the question before the Delhi High Court, where both companies argue Indian law doesn't require platforms to proactively monitor or block unauthorised court recordings. The outcome could redefine Section 79, safe harbour, and intermediary liability in India.

 The answer is more nuanced than you think.

From Section 69A of the IT Act to government blocking orders, platform guidelines, and intermediary safe-harbour protection-there's an important legal distinction every competitive exam aspirant should know.

text:
🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

MAHARASHTRA CYBER CAN DETECT DEEPFAKES IN 10 SECONDS

AI-generated videos can look incredibly real, making it difficult to know what is genuine and what has been manipulated.

> Maharashtra Cyber has advanced digital-forensics capabilities for analysing and authenticating audio and video, including deepfake detection. 

> The technology can help investigators examine suspicious videos and identify signs of manipulation.

> So if someone is using an AI-generated video to defame, threaten or blackmail you, don’t stay silent.

> Preserve the original video and other evidence, and contact the police or cyber authorities.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

I sized a position on a thin order book once and watched my own buy order become the top of it, lol

Price ran up before I even finished filling.....
nobody manipulated anything...

I just didn't understand what I was looking at.

took me way too long to learn the word for it: "Spread".

Here's the thing nobody really explains early enough 

A market never has one price, It has two:
>the highest price someone's willing to pay (the bid) 
>and the lowest price someone's willing to sell for (the ask) 

the gap between them is the spread, and it's basically the market grading its own liquidity in real time

Tight spread usually means the book is deep. you can put size in and the price barely move. Wide spread means the book is thin, and the second you place an order, you're not trading against the market anymore....you are the market

your own order becomes exposed to volatility 

Every crypto trader has felt this, you buy a low cap you're excited about and the price you get is nowhere near the price you saw on the chart two seconds earlier. 

that's not the app lying to you...that's the Spread doing exactly what it's supposed to do.

The part that took me longest to get is the fact that this isn't a crypto quirk. 

It's the same mechanic on Apple stock, on Gold, on every market on earth 

Nobody sets the price of any of it. It's a nonstop auction between buyers and sellers, and the spread is just the most honest number on your screen telling you how much the market can actually absorb before it notices you.

So you always have to check the spread before you size....Not after.

A Bridge Too Far is probably the most faithful big budget war epic of its era, and the reason is that Attenborough was adapting Cornelius Ryan's 1974 book, which was built out of hundreds of interviews with men who were actually there. Several of them, including John Frost, Roy Urquhart and Brian Horrocks, were consulted on the film. So the skeleton is real. The three division chain, the single road, the blown bridge at Son, the radios failing, the drop zones sited miles from the objective, Frost holding the north end of Arnhem bridge and nothing else, the Waal crossing in canvas boats, the resupply drifting down onto German held ground, the Polish brigade arriving late and on the wrong bank, the withdrawal across the Rhine in the rain. All of that happened, roughly in that order, roughly for those reasons.

Some of the small details people assume are Hollywood are the real ones. Major Digby Tatham-Warter really did go into battle with an umbrella. Kate ter Horst really did turn her house into a dressing station and read psalms to dying men. The Dutch surgeon Spaander is real. The sergeant who pulls a pistol on a surgeon to get his officer operated on comes straight out of Ryan's interviews. The German commanders being competent, quick and professional rather than cartoonish is accurate and was unusual for the time.

Where it drifts is mostly in emphasis and blame. The film is heavily invested in making Boy Browning the villain. The famous line about a bridge too far is presented as a warning Browning gave before the operation, and the sourcing for that is thin. Ryan got it late, second hand, and it may well have been said afterward if it was said at all. Browning's family, including Daphne du Maurier, were furious about the portrayal, and modern historians generally think he has been made to carry weight that belongs further up the chain. Montgomery barely appears in the film. The man whose plan it was, whose reputation it was meant to restore, and who later called it ninety percent successful, is essentially absent from the story of its failure.

The intelligence officer who gets sidelined for warning about SS armor is a composite. In the film he is Major Fuller. In life it was Brian Urquhart, Browning's intelligence officer, no relation to the general, and he was packed off on medical leave for being insistent. The substance is accurate. The name and the scene are not.

The film also inflates the German armor. Watching it you come away thinking two full SS panzer divisions were sitting at Arnhem waiting. They were badly chewed up formations refitting after Normandy, closer to battlegroups than divisions, with a limited number of running tanks. What actually killed the British was not mass but reaction speed. Bittrich had blocking units moving within hours. That is a more interesting and more damning fact than the one the film gives you, because it means the operation lost to improvisation rather than to a hidden army.

XXX Corps comes off worst of anyone. The film leans hard on the image of Guards tanks halted and brewing tea while men die up the road, and that image has done real damage to the historical reputation of a corps that was taking casualties the whole way up a road it could not leave. The halt at Nijmegen after the Waal crossing is genuinely controversial and historians still argue it, but the film frames it as complacency rather than as a unit out of infantry, out of daylight and sitting on an exposed embankment. Likewise Gavin's decision to secure the Groesbeek heights before pushing into Nijmegen is never really explained, so the American delay looks like carelessness instead of a defensible call about his own flank.

The biggest structural distortion is proportional. The film is about the bridge, and the bridge was over by Thursday. Most of 1st Airborne died in the Oosterbeek perimeter afterward, in a nine day battle that gets a fraction of the screen time. And the film ends with civilians walking out of the ruins, which is moving, but it skips what came next for them. The Hunger Winter killed roughly twenty thousand Dutch civilians north of the rivers who had been told liberation was days away.

If you want the corrective reading, Middlebrook's Arnhem 1944 is the detailed operational account, Robert Kershaw's It Never Snows in September gives you the German side properly, and Beevor's Arnhem is the modern argument that the plan was unsound at conception rather than unlucky in execution. Ryan is still worth reading, just understand that he was writing a human mosaic, not an operational analysis, and the film inherited both the strength and the limitation of that.

It’s not about finding evidence to support an argument. It’s about testing claims against the evidence.

⚖️ Independent & non-partisan
🔎 Evidence-led
📚 Transparent sources & corrections

Sometimes the evidence is clear. Sometimes it isn’t. Our job is to explain what it can, and cannot, tell us.

Section 16 of the DPDP Act lets the Government bar transfers of personal data to named countries. No country has been named, so personal data may leave India freely today.

The direction is the reverse of GDPR, which blocks transfers until a destination is approved. A section 16 notification needs no consultation and carries no transition period, and sectoral rules such as the RBI's payment data directive continue to apply regardless.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

(Source - FinFloww on Whatsapp)

Have you noticed this?

A lot of things don't become expensive overnight.

First, they're free. Then you start using them regularly. Then, somewhere along the way, you start paying for them without thinking twice.

We've seen this happen everywhere in India-

Jio gave us ridiculously cheap data.
We stopped thinking twice before using it.

UPI made digital payments effortless.
Now the ecosystem around payments is becoming a business opportunity.

Food delivery apps gave us free delivery and heavy discounts.
We stopped calling the restaurant. Then came delivery fees, platform fees and all the other little charges.

OTT platforms started with cheap subscriptions and free trials.
Now every cricket match, movie and series seems to have its own platform.

Banks gave us zero-balance accounts and free services.
Over time, minimum balances, ATM limits and various service charges became normal.

The interesting part isn't the charge. It's the timing. Nobody wants to pay for something they don't use.

So first, get them to use it. Then use it often. Then make it convenient. Then make it a habit. And only then put a price on it.

It's not a new trick. Product, technology, generation, everything else changes.

But, the sequence has remained remarkably consistent:
Free → Habit → Dependence → Monetisation.

Sometimes, the smartest price is ₹0 at the beginning.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

Who most easily can mess with machines? IT.  I saw and blew the whistle on that when I worked in state government.  And Steve Trout gave us a heads up on that in the 2020 election.

From the beginning in the 1990s when computers came into government agencies managers were "editing" and "deleting" data to make it look like to the legislature that these unelected failed managers were doing as directed by the legislature through passing laws.  IT helped them by unlocking "locked down records".

Thus, when managers were deleting records the unique number still could be seen.  What happened with my report?  IT sent an email to all of us saying that they "fixed that glitch" and now the unique number was hidden.  That's how cavalier these managers are in violating law. It's the upper and mid-managers in power in these governmental structures. Hey everyone and @SamsungIndia Story start from 23 April 2026 till today, I have been trapped in what feels like a complete service scam by Samsung’s authorized service centre in Dharampeth, Nagpur, Maharashtra.

I discovered a sudden issue in the 0.6x ultra-wide camera of my Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra. The phone was never dropped, never mishandled. After researching online, I found MANY users reporting the exact same issue with the new 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Reddit, YouTube, Samsung Community — same problem everywhere.

Because my device was out of warranty, the Dharampeth service centre immediately gave me a ₹4000 quotation instead of acknowledging a possible manufacturing defect.

After endless emails, Samsung support kept repeating: “You have to pay.”

Why should customers pay for Samsung’s hardware failure?

After getting exhausted, I posted on X on 26 April tagging Samsung Electronics India. Only then did they react. Customer Experience Manager Kajal contacted me, and after I shared proof from multiple users online, Samsung finally offered a 73% discount.

I accepted because I was mentally tired of fighting.

On 6 May, I submitted the device. On 7 May, I collected it after paying ₹1000.

Camera fixed?
YES.

New disaster?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF THE VERY NEXT MORNING.

I informed the service centre on WhatsApp. They ignored the messages.

Visited again on 11 May — they “fixed” it.

Two days later?
BACK PANEL AGAIN COMING OFF.

Visited again on 14 May — this time the behavior became shocking.

Instead of accepting poor repair quality, staff started accusing ME of removing the back panel with sharp objects. They checked the device and found ZERO evidence.

Then they saw BGMI installed.

And suddenly their excuse became:
“BGMI is a third-party app. Using third-party apps voids warranty and service.”

Imagine buying one of Samsung’s most powerful flagship phones and being told GAMING can void service support.

When I asked for a written denial letter, they REFUSED.

When I started recording for proof, they stopped answering questions and began ignoring me completely.

I had no option left except calling the police.

ONLY after police intervention did the entire attitude of the service centre change. Suddenly:
“We never denied service.”
“We are ready to repair.”

They even requested police officers to convince me to delete the videos I recorded.

After another repair attempt, they told me:
“Do not use BGMI for 12 hours.”

I followed everything they said.

Result?
BACK PANEL STARTED COMING OFF AGAIN.

Since then I have been continuously emailing Samsung support and Kajal from customer experience, asking for a permanent solution or replacement because I cannot travel 13KM repeatedly for the SAME ISSUE.

Today again, after being told to visit the service centre, they AGAIN accused me and AGAIN refused service while refusing to provide any written denial.

The moment I started recording, everyone went silent.

This is the reality of Samsung’s “premium flagship experience” in Nagpur.

Customers are blamed.
Manufacturing defects are ignored.
Poor repairs are repeated.
Written denials are refused.
And consumers are forced into endless visits until they give up.

Absolutely shameful. @SamsungMobile @SamsungIndia
